1.point: Open with the Munajat's confession and tell the reader the chapter will show why knowing ourselves is the way to knowing our Lord, and how.
steps: A familiar prayer confesses neglect of the soul
The soul was given into our care and can be neglected
It deserves care because it is the means by which we know anything
The soul knows itself directly, by presence, the clearest case of such knowing
Knowing God (not about Him) needs that same direct knowing, so it happens in the soul; the chapter will show why and how

2.point: The Qur'an (al-Shams) makes a person's success or failure turn on whether the soul is purified or betrayed.
steps: Al-Shams swears by the soul and the discernment God placed in it
The verses that follow make success and failure depend on what is done with that soul
So the human story is the soul's story

3.point: Knowing God starts with knowing the soul, because forgetting God loses the soul and knowing the soul shows its Lord.
steps: Forgetting God makes a person forget the soul (al-Hashr)
So remembering God brings attention back to the soul
Losing the soul in turn loses faith (al-An'am), because a soul that is seen points to its Maker
The saying 'whoever knows himself knows his Lord' states the two-way link
The saying holds because the soul reflects its Maker without being part of Him
Therefore knowing God begins with knowing the soul

4.point: God is near now; what separates us is a veil over our own soul, and it must be lifted in this life because what we see of Him later depends on what we see now.
steps: We are already in God's presence but do not perceive it
So reaching Him is removing a veil over the heart, not travelling
Every soul's veils come off at the promised meeting after death, where each sees its own soul
What is seen then depends on what is seen now
So the seeker starts lifting the veils in this life; the way to God runs through the self

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: The hook: a prayer the reader knows contains a confession, which the chapter will unpack.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Reads the confession: the soul was given into our care and can be neglected. Sets up why care is owed.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Why the soul deserves care: it is the means of all our knowing. Needed for ¶5's 'every other study is carried out with it'.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Introduces knowledge by presence, the soul's direct self-knowledge; ¶5 relies on it ('this same direct knowing'). Longer than the two-sentence recall the point allows, but each sentence is used.

¶5.label: advance
¶5.why: States the chapter's thesis in the words of the title: knowing God must happen in the soul, so we must know ourselves to know our Lord.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: Sets up al-Shams: the oath by the soul and the gift of discernment, which the following verses build on.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Draws the verses' consequence: success or failure turns on purifying or betraying the soul. This is the section's point.

¶8.label: restate
¶8.why: 'The whole story of a human being is the story of the soul' says again what ¶7 established; the Munajat link is a callback to the opening, not a new step.

¶9.label: advance
¶9.why: First link: losing the soul has a cause named by al-Hashr, forgetting God.

¶10.label: aside
¶10.why: Softens the verse's 'transgressors' and glosses forgetting as not realising potential. Nothing later uses this; ¶11's cure follows from the verse, not from this paragraph.

¶11.label: advance
¶11.why: The reverse direction: remembering God turns attention back to the soul. One half of 'forgotten together, known together'.

¶12.label: advance
¶12.why: Adds the other causal direction: losing the soul loses faith, with al-An'am as the warrant.

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Explains why losing the soul loses faith: a soul that is seen shows its Creator in a way the body does not. This mechanism carries ¶15 and section 4.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Brings the two directions together and introduces the saying that states the link in one line. The first sentence is a brief summary, but the saying is a step the section needs.

¶15.label: advance
¶15.why: Grounds the saying: the soul reflects its Maker, with the needed guard that it is not part of God.

¶16.label: advance
¶16.why: Draws the conclusion that is the section's point. The Tabataba'i quotation is a second authority, but its 'window of the soul' image is what section 4 picks up in 'looking within'.

¶17.label: advance
¶17.why: First step of the section: God is already near; what we lack is perception of Him.

¶18.label: advance
¶18.why: So reaching God is removing a veil over the heart, not travelling; defines hijab and qurb that the rest of the section uses.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: Introduces the meeting after death at which every soul's veils come off, which the argument for 'in this life' needs.

¶20.label: advance
¶20.why: Says what the meeting is: the layers over the soul are removed and each sees its own soul. Repeats 'every soul' from ¶19 but adds the step ¶21 and ¶23 build on.

¶21.label: support
¶21.why: Explains how seeing one's own soul counts as a meeting with God (the soul is His reflection), which ¶20 asserts. The believer/unbeliever sentence is not used again.

¶22.label: aside
¶22.why: A limit (the soul cannot encompass God, with Khomeini confirming) that the point does not need; nothing in ¶23 to ¶26 depends on it.

¶23.label: advance
¶23.why: The decisive step for 'in this life': what the soul perceives of God then depends on what it perceives now.

¶24.label: advance
¶24.why: Draws the conclusion that the seeker starts now, adds a second reason, and ties the mystics' methods to the one aim of removing the veil.

¶25.label: aside
¶25.why: A second scholar describing the uncovered self and tying it to the saying already quoted in section 3; ¶26 does not depend on it.

¶26.label: restate
¶26.why: Summarises ¶17, ¶18 and section 3; the way runs through the self has already been reached in ¶24.

¶27.label: aside
¶27.why: A bridging question for the next chapter; the section's argument does not use it.
